transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Liam (Veridian Head of AI), Priya (Infra Engineer), Derek (Product)

Summary (auto): 52m POC scoping: focused on unit economics, sample workload sizing, benchmarking plan, and timelines. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot benchmark after Veridian provides a 24h traffic slice and sample prompts. Primary success: < $0.002/token effective cost at 95th latency under 600ms for 95% of requests; throughput target 500 QPS sustained for hotspot flows.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for making time. um quick roll call and then we can jump in. Maya here, AE on the account, Ethan's our solutions lead.
[00:12] Liam (Veridian): hey all, Liam here. excited to dig in.
[00:15] Priya (Veridian): Priya on infra.
[00:18] Derek (Veridian): Derek, product.
[00:20] Ethan (Redwood SE): hi, Ethan. quick agenda — sizing, target SLOs, what success looks like, then bench plan and timeline. sound good?
[00:30] Liam: yep, go for it.

[00:45] Maya: first, high level: Veridian wants to add a generative assistant inside checkout and support questions, and we heard the rough numbers — is that still accurate, Liam, like 300k active users, peaks at 700 qps internal?
[00:58] Liam: yeah that's about right; core flows probably 400 to 600 qps during promos, baseline 120 qps. average session is short, 1-3 prompts, but some flows have long context — like 600 tokens prompt, 400 tokens response sometimes. so average roundtrip maybe 250–300 tokens.
[01:20] Ethan: okay great. for cost modeling we care about average tokens per request, distribution (p50/p95), and QPS shape over day — so those numbers help.

[01:40] Priya: our infra constraint is we can't have more than 10ms of additional request overhead in our edge services. we also need data to stay in-us-east-1. VPC peering is fine.
[01:53] Maya: got it — we'll note data residency and VPC-only for the pilot.

[02:10] Derek: what are realistic per-token estimates? we've been eyeballing vendor numbers but want a grounded plan.

[02:18] Ethan: okay quick framing — cost/unit depends on model choice, batch size, prefix or KV cache hit rate, and whether we use hosted vs dedicated GPUs. as a ballpark: for a 13B-ish open model quantized to int8 on a T4-like host, you might see ~$0.0008 to $0.0015 per token in hosted, but you can get down to ~$0.0004–0.0007 with dedicated capacity and aggressive batching/caching. those ranges are fuzzy — bench will nail it down.

[02:55] Liam: wow that's a broad range. what drives the difference mainly?

[03:00] Ethan: batching is huge — if your latency SLO allows larger batches, throughput token-cost goes down. caching — if many requests share prefixes or repeated system prompts, KV/prefix cache reduces repeated compute for earlier layers. also sequence length: longer responses cost more linearly. and kernel optimizations / quantization matter too.

[03:25] Priya: can you explain KV cache vs prefix cache? we've heard the terms but they get mixed in our notes.

[03:30] Ethan: sure. kv cache is the runtime cache of keys/values for a single conversation token history so repeated tokens in the same ongoing session are faster. prefix caching is storing the activations for common system or few-shot prefixes across requests so you don't recompute them every time. in practice, prefix hits can cut avg token compute by 20–60% depending on your prompt patterns. (murmur: sometimes transcribed as K V cash)

[04:05] Derek: do you have a recommended knob set to test? like specific batch sizes and cache hit target?

[04:10] Ethan: yes — suggestion: run three bench scenarios: 1) conservative low-latency: batch size 1–4, no prefix cache, simulate p95 latency goal 250–400ms; 2) balanced: batch 8–16, prefix cache enabled, target p95 400–600ms; 3) throughput-optimized: batch 32+, aggressive prefix caching (and dedicated capacity), target cost-min and p95 up to 900ms if acceptable. we'll measure tokens/sec, p95 latency, and effective $/1M tokens.

[04:55] Maya: from a business POV, what's your budget target? Derek or Liam?
[05:02] Derek: we want predictable runway — ideally the assistant costs less than $0.10 per MAU in the first year. tough to map that to tokens without baseline usage patterns.

[05:12] Liam: goal also to be cheaper than building our own serving stack while keeping latency acceptable.

[05:20] Ethan: okay we'll convert the scenarios into per-MAU math once we have traffic sample. rough example: if average user triggers 2 requests/day at 300 tokens each that's 600 tokens/user/day ~ 18k tokens/month per MAU; at $0.0006/token that's ~$10.8/month — so clearly we need tighter numbers. that's why bench is crucial. (note: math is approximate)

[06:00] Priya: uh, that math seems off compared to our expectations — can you rewalk?

[06:05] Ethan: sure. sorry I rushed — 600 tokens/day * 30 = 18k tokens/month; multiply by $0.0006 gives $10.8, yes, that's per monthly active user. so if your target is $0.10/MAU we need per-token to be ~0.000006, which is unrealistic. So, either usage per user is much lower, or we have to limit features, or use strong caching and rate-limits.

[06:35] Liam: okay that clarifies tradeoffs: product may need lower calls per user or we target a subset of users for assistant. good to know.

[06:50] Maya: for the pilot, let's keep the scope to critical checkout helper flows (higher dollars AOV) so ROI is clearer. and we'll target the balanced scenario as default.

[07:05] Derek: timeline question: how long to get a reliable per-token number?

[07:10] Ethan: plan is: once Veridian sends a 24h representative traffic slice and ~50 example prompt/response pairs, we set up a bench harness and run 48–72 hour runs across the three scenarios. initial results in 7–10 days, then a 2-week pilot if you want long tail.

[07:28] Priya: do you run bench on our VPC or in-hosted Redwood?

[07:33] Maya: for scoping we can do hosted to get baseline numbers quickly, but we'll run an on-VPC private pilot for any production-like test. Redwood Private can be deployed into your cloud account for the pilot.

[07:47] Liam: is there any code we need to change? minimal integration is nice.

[07:51] Ethan: minimal — the bench uses an HTTP shim and simulates the request patterns. for pilot with VPC we'll share an integration guide; typically a small sidecar or a forwarding layer. Priya, you'll probably only need to open a couple routes and certs.

[08:10] Derek: security/compliance — we need to know SOC2 coverage and where logs go.

[08:15] Maya: we are SOC2 Type II and we can provide the report. for pilot logs we can route audit logs to your splunk/elastic, and sensitive payloads can be redacted or configured to not leave the VPC. we'll attach security docs in the follow-up.

[08:32] Priya: great, we'll want the compliance contact.

[08:35] Maya: will include that.

[08:40] Ethan: back to bench knobs — we also recommend measuring cache hit curves. e.g., run with prefix cache miss at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% to emulate real patterns. that tells you marginal gains.

[08:55] Liam: how do you capture cost back to product? unit econ calc I want to put in a one-pager for execs.

[09:02] Ethan: we'll provide a simple spreadsheet: inputs (avg prompt tokens, avg response tokens, qps, pct cached, batch size) and outputs (tokens/sec, effective $/1M tokens, avg latency p50/p95). we'll fill it with bench results and produce a recommended operating point.

[09:20] Derek: okay. are there any gotchas we should be aware of when measuring?

[09:24] Ethan: yes — synthetic tests can overstate batching gains if they don't mimic the natural arrival process. also warm vs cold cache; and if you test on small instances you might hit networking limits. we ask for the 24h real traffic to replay arrival patterns.

[09:40] Maya: question for Veridian: what's the decision criteria? aside from cost per MAU, any SLA/latency hard stops?

[09:48] Liam: product wants p95 < 600ms for checkout assistant. infra needs region residency and SSO. finance will approve if cost projection shows positive unit economics within 3 months per pilot.

[10:05] Maya: alright, so primary success: p95 < 600ms, effective cost <$0.0007/token for the target flows, and smooth integration in VPC. agree?

[10:14] Derek: yes agree.

[10:18] Priya: agree but add that we need ability to redact payloads before any logs leave our VPC.

[10:25] Ethan: noted — redaction step supported.

[10:30] Liam: one more question — any fallback strategy if you hit capacity spikes?

[10:37] Maya: yes, Redwood has smart routing and fallbacks — you can route to a lighter, cheaper model or allow degraded responses with cached answers. also burst capacity options. we'll show config examples.

[10:50] Derek: for the benchmark, can we include an OpenAI comparison?

[10:55] Ethan: yes, we can run the same harness against OpenAI endpoints and show cost/latency delta, though you'll need your OpenAI creds for that.

[11:05] Liam: we'll provide.

[11:10] Priya: ok timing — let's aim to have the 24h traffic slice and sample prompts by 2026-09-15, then initial bench results by 2026-09-24. pilot kickoff week of 2026-09-27?

[11:22] Maya: that timeline works for us.

[11:28] Ethan: implementation detail — we'll capture tokenization differences between models. sometimes token counts change meaningfully between model families and that impacts cost.

[11:38] Derek: good point.

[11:42] Maya: any other questions, concerns?

[11:45] Liam: just one concern — if we go dedicated, how long is lead time for GPUs? procurement wants to know.

[11:52] Ethan: Dedicated capacity can be provisioned in weeks not months depending on region; for pilot we often use hosted + reserved instances to simulate dedicated throughput. we'll provide a provisioning timeline in the worksheet.

[12:08] Priya: also, we need to know the rollout pattern in case we want canary.

[12:12] Maya: Redwood supports canary and traffic-split rollouts; we'll include a recommended strategy in the runbook.

[12:20] Derek: ok great.

[12:25] Ethan: last technical note — if your prompts include private PII fields, please flag them; we can provide field-level redaction or keep those requests on-prem.

[12:36] Liam: will do.

[12:40] Maya: recap of next steps: Maya will send pricing worksheet; Ethan will send benchmark harness and sample scripts; Priya/Liam will share traffic slice and prompts; schedule kickoff. action items are in the doc.

[12:55] Derek: perfect. thanks all.

[13:00] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and links to the security pack. bye.

(End of transcript)

Notes: occasional auto-caption glitches observed ("K V cash" for KV cache, "vee-pic" for VPC). The transcript has filler words and some speaker overlap.
